trial_name: FEAST — Mortality after Fluid Bolus in African Children with Severe Infection (2011)
journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
citation: Maitland K, Kiguli S, Opoka RO, et al. Mortality after Fluid Bolus in African Children with Severe Infection. N Engl J Med. 2011;364(26):2483–2495
one_liner: In African children with severe febrile illness and impaired perfusion, fluid boluses with albumin or saline increased 48-hour mortality compared to no bolus.

pico.population: African children aged >60 days to <12 years admitted with severe febrile illness and signs of impaired perfusion.
pico.intervention: Fluid bolus therapy with 5% human albumin solution or 0.9% saline (20–40 mL/kg over 1 hour).
pico.comparison: No fluid bolus control (maintenance fluids only; rescue saline given only if hypotensive shock developed).
pico.outcome: Primary outcome was all-cause mortality at 48 hours; secondary outcomes included 4-week mortality, neurological sequelae, and safety events.

background.existing_knowledge: Rapid fluid bolus therapy was standard in paediatric shock algorithms based on physiological extrapolation and high-resource critical care practice.
background.knowledge_gap: In low-resource African hospital settings with high rates of malaria and severe anaemia and limited ICU facilities, it was unknown whether fluid boluses improved survival or caused harm.
background.hypothesis: Fluid bolus therapy (albumin or saline) reduces 48-hour mortality compared with no bolus in children with severe febrile illness and impaired perfusion, and albumin is superior to saline.

methods.design: Multicentre, open-label, randomised controlled trial stopped early for harm by the DSMB.
methods.setting: District hospitals in Africa; enrolled patients across two strata (FEAST A without severe hypotension, FEAST B with hypotensive shock).

inclusion: History of fever and/or abnormal temperature (pyrexia >=37.5°C or hypothermia <36°C)
Severe illness (>=1): impaired consciousness (prostration or coma) or respiratory distress (deep breathing or increased work of breathing)

Impaired perfusion (>=1): capillary refill >2 seconds, lower limb temperature gradient, weak radial pulse volume, or severe tachycardia (HR >180 bpm if <12 months; >160 bpm if 12 months–5 years; >140 bpm if >5 years)
Strata FEAST A: impaired perfusion without severe hypotension (3 arms: albumin vs saline vs no bolus)
Strata FEAST B: hypotensive shock (2 arms: albumin vs saline; severe SBP <50 mmHg if <12 months, <60 mmHg if 12 months–5 years, <70 mmHg if >5 years plus >=1 sign of impaired perfusion)
exclusion: Severe acute malnutrition (visible severe wasting and/or kwashiorkor)
Gastroenteritis (>3 watery stools in the previous 24 hours)
Contraindications to volume expansion (chronic renal failure, pulmonary oedema with SpO2 <90% plus bilateral basal crepitations)
Prior isotonic volume expansion during current illness

methods.intervention: 5% human albumin solution or 0.9% saline administered over 1 hour. FEAST A initial bolus 20 mL/kg; at 1 hour, repeat 20 mL/kg if impaired perfusion persisted, or 40 mL/kg if hypotensive shock developed. FEAST B initial bolus 40 mL/kg; repeat 20–40 mL/kg at 1 hour if perfusion deficit/shock persisted. Protocolised 24-hour maximum volume limit: 80 mL/kg.
methods.comparison: No bolus control in FEAST A (low-volume maintenance fluids per national guidelines). Rescue 0.9% saline 40 mL/kg over 1 hour was administered only if hypotensive shock developed.
methods.blinding: Open-label (unblinded) treatment allocation; primary endpoint (mortality) was objective.
methods.sample_size_power: Trial monitored independently with prespecified stopping rules; DSMB recommended early termination due to excess mortality in bolus groups.
secondary_outcomes: Pulmonary oedema or raised intracranial pressure
methods.follow_up: 48 hours primary endpoint; follow-up continued to 4 weeks.

headline_bullets: Fluid bolus therapy (saline or albumin) significantly increased 48-hour mortality compared with no bolus.
Albumin conferred no mortality benefit over 0.9% saline.
Classic fluid overload features (pulmonary oedema / raised ICP) were rare and did not explain the increased mortality.

safety: Pulmonary oedema or raised ICP occurred in 2.4% (50/2097) in any bolus group vs 1.7% (18/1044) in control (p=0.12).
New neurological sequelae at discharge occurred in 2.1% (44/2097) vs 2.0% (21/1044) (p=0.92).

domains.notes: Large, multicentre randomised design with robust protocolisation and prospective outcome ascertainment.
Open-label design; however, primary endpoint (mortality) is objective and immune to detection bias.
Intention-to-treat analysis with complete outcome ascertainment.
Rescue saline (40 mL/kg) administered to control group children who developed hypotensive shock per protocol.
Well-balanced baseline characteristics across study arms.

internal_validity.verdict: High internal validity for primary mortality endpoint given robust multicentre randomisation and objective endpoint.

domains.notes: Highly representative of severely ill febrile children presenting to African hospitals with impaired perfusion, high malaria burden, and severe anaemia.
Conducted in resource-limited settings without advanced PICU supportive care (mechanical ventilation, central lines, vasoactive infusions).

external_validity.verdict: Strong generalisability to low-resource settings, but extrapolation to high-resource PICU contexts or dehydration phenotypes is limited.

strengths: Large pragmatic multicentre RCT with 3,141 children enrolled
Objective, clinically relevant primary endpoint (48-hour mortality)
Direct comparison of colloid (albumin) versus crystalloid (saline) and no bolus control
High rate of complete follow-up to 4 weeks
limitations: Stopped early for harm by DSMB
Lack of advanced supportive critical care modalities (invasive ventilation, vasoactive drugs)
Excluded gastroenteritis and severe acute malnutrition, limiting applicability to pure dehydration

critical_appraisal.summary: High-quality, landmark RCT demonstrating clear early mortality harm from rapid fluid boluses in African children with severe febrile illness and impaired perfusion.
strengths: Large sample size and multicentre design
Rigorous trial oversight and objective primary endpoint
Clear prospective hypothesis testing of colloid vs crystalloid vs control
weaknesses: Early termination may overestimate magnitude of effect
Absence of mechanical ventilation and inotropes limits direct translation to high-resource PICU settings

sections.authors_conclusion: Fluid boluses with saline or albumin significantly increased 48-hour mortality compared with no bolus control in African children with severe febrile illness and impaired perfusion.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Avoid routine rapid IV fluid boluses in children presenting with severe febrile illness and impaired perfusion in low-resource settings without mechanical ventilation and vasoactive support.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Pediatric patients in resource-limited settings presenting with severe febrile illness, impaired perfusion, malaria, or severe anaemia without frank hypotensive shock.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Do not give IV fluids for diarrhoeal dehydration or severe acute malnutrition; FEAST explicitly excluded these groups.
implementation_caveats: Hypotensive shock still warrants targeted volume expansion per protocol.
Rehydration strategies in gastroenteritis and severe malnutrition are supported by separate evidence.

controversies.notes: High-resource guidelines still recommend fluid boluses for septic shock where invasive monitoring, mechanical ventilation, and vasoactive drugs are immediately available.
Excess deaths were not driven by pulmonary oedema or raised ICP, but rather early cardiovascular collapse following bolus administration.
Global guideline adoption of FEAST findings in low-resource settings has been variable and contentious.

context_related_trials.relation: Evaluated IV rehydration strategies in non-malnourished children with severe diarrhoeal dehydration, demonstrating no mortality harm.
Evaluated IV rehydration strategies in children with severe acute malnutrition and dehydrating gastroenteritis, confirming no mortality harm signal.

unresolved_questions: Mechanism explaining rapid cardiovascular collapse after fluid boluses in normotensive severe infection.
Safety and efficacy of small-volume slow fluid administration vs early vasoactive agent initiation in low-resource pediatric shock.

numbers_to_remember: Albumin vs Saline mortality identical: 10.6% vs 10.5% (RR 1.01)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In low-resource pediatric severe febrile illness, rapid fluid boluses cause early mortality from cardiovascular collapse, not fluid overload, and should be avoided.
